intro: Twenty years after his New York recording, Paderewski returns to this nocturne in London. The F♯-major song and its restless middle are still in his hands in January 1937, just before his appearance on cinema screens in Moonlight Sonata.

sections.label: A · The decorated F♯-major melody
sections.mNote: The left hand steps between low notes and chords

sections.label: B · Doppio movimento, sotto voce
sections.mNote: A dotted tune and quick notes share the right hand

sections.label: C · The slow melody returns
sections.mNote: The opening upbeat returns after the quick figures subside

sections.label: D · F♯ and the last flourishes
sections.mNote: Descending groups of small notes, marked smorzando

cues.title: A bass below the singer
cues.text: The left hand makes a small circuit: low bass, higher note, chord, higher note again. Above it, the right hand’s melody pauses on long notes and slips into quick flourishes. The opening marking is sostenuto, sustained.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, upbeat and bars 1–4. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two jobs for one hand
cues.text: The right hand now carries a dotted melody and a busy line underneath it. The left hand jumps below both. Doppio movimento doubles the pace; sotto voce asks for a subdued beginning.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–32. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the Larghetto
cues.text: The quick figures slow down and dwindle. After a pause, the opening tune resumes its old pace. Chopin writes fresh ornaments into the reprise, then sends small notes tumbling towards the final F♯.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–62: slowing, pause, a Tempo and the decorated closing section. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paderewski on the screen
cues.text: In February 1937, Moonlight Sonata brings Paderewski into British cinemas. He plays himself in a romance involving a forced landing and a Swedish baroness. The camera also stays with him at the piano for Beethoven’s slow movement and his own Minuet.
cues.evidence: The film opens on 11 February 1937: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlight_Sonata_(film). Chicago Film Archives describes its preserved performance excerpts: https://collections.chicagofilmarchives.org/Detail/objects/2737

cues.title: The last small notes
cues.text: Groups of tiny notes run down through the F♯ harmony. Chopin writes smorzando — dying away — over the final descent. The bass settles on a low F♯, with A♯ left above it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 60–62, including the smorzando descent and final F♯–A♯. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
